lead: One mole of ethanol added to a large tank of water does not change the volume by the same amount as one mole of pure ethanol. The surroundings change what each molecule can do. A partial molar property measures the real contribution of one component to a mixture property while temperature, pressure and all other amounts stay fixed. It converts measured mixture data into component properties for chemical potential, phase equilibrium and energy balances.
prereq: You need chemical potential and partial derivatives taken with T and P fixed.

blocks.text: Take a mixture with total moles n and n<sub>i</sub> moles of component i. Let M be any molar property: volume, enthalpy, entropy or Gibbs energy. The total property is nM, an extensive quantity. A partial molar property M̄<sub>i</sub> answers one question: how fast does nM change, per mole of i, when a very small amount of i is added with T, P and every other n<sub>j</sub> fixed? The definition is:

blocks.where: M is any molar property of the mixture; n is total moles; n<sub>i</sub> is moles of component i; n<sub>j</sub> means all other mole numbers held fixed; T is temperature and P is pressure.

blocks.text: M̄<sub>i</sub> has the same units as M (for example cm³/mol for volume). For a pure component it equals the ordinary molar property. In a mixture it depends on composition. Adding the contributions of all components gives the mixture property:

blocks.where: M is the mixture molar property; x<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction of component i; M̄<sub>i</sub> is its partial molar property; the sum runs over all components.

blocks.text: The sum M = Σ xi M̄i uses partial molar values at the actual composition, not pure-component values. The Gibbs energy case is special: Ḡi = μi, the chemical potential, as in Chapter 5.1.

For a binary mixture, plot M against x₁ at fixed T and P. Draw the tangent at the chosen composition. Extend it to x₁ = 1 and x₁ = 0. The intercept at x₁ = 1 is M̄₁; the intercept at x₁ = 0 is M̄₂. This tangent-intercept construction reads both partial molar properties from one curve.

blocks.where: M̄₁ is the partial molar property of component 1; M is the mixture molar property; x₂ is the mole fraction of component 2; dM/dx₁ is the slope of M against x₁ at fixed T and P.
M̄₂ is the partial molar property of component 2; M is the mixture molar property; x₁ is the mole fraction of component 1; dM/dx₁ is the slope of M against x₁ at fixed T and P.

blocks.text: Here x₂ = 1 − x₁ and dM/dx₁ is the slope of the M curve at the chosen composition. The slope equals M̄₁ − M̄₂. The figure uses V = 18 + 28x₁ − 6x₁². At x₁ = 0.25, V = 24.625 cm³/mol and dV/dx₁ = 28 − 12(0.25) = 25.0 cm³/mol. The tangent is 18.375 + 25x₁; its intercepts are V̄₂ = 18.375 and V̄₁ = 43.375 cm³/mol.

sections.h3: Volume, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy

blocks.text: Each property has its own partial molar version. V̄<sub>i</sub> is the partial molar volume, used in mixture density and volume change on mixing. H̄<sub>i</sub> is the partial molar enthalpy, used in heat effects. S̄<sub>i</sub> is the partial molar entropy, used in entropy balances. Ḡ<sub>i</sub> is the partial molar Gibbs energy, equal to μ<sub>i</sub>. All four change with composition.

Use the values at the composition of the mixture. A pure-component table gives Vi, Hi or Si only at xi = 1. At x₁ = 0.25 in the example, V̄₁ = 43.375 and V̄₂ = 18.375 cm³/mol. At another x₁, recompute both. The changes are linked by the Gibbs-Duhem equation in Chapter 5.3.

Partial molar properties appear in energy balances, phase-equilibrium calculations and property estimates. Later, activity coefficients are built from partial molar Gibbs energies, and VLE data reduction uses partial molar volumes.

figure.caption: The worked example on the V–x₁ curve. The tangent at x₁ = 0.25 (slope 25.0 cm³/mol) cuts x₁ = 0 at V̄₂ = 18.375 and x₁ = 1 at V̄₁ = 43.375 cm³/mol; pure component 1 has V = 40, less than V̄₁ at this composition.

examples.question: For a binary liquid mixture at 298 K and 1 bar, the molar volume is V = 40x₁ + 18x₂ + 6x₁x₂ cm³/mol, where x₁ and x₂ are mole fractions. Find V̄₁ and V̄₂ at x₁ = 0.25.
steps: Differentiate with x₂ = 1 − x₁: V = 18 + 22x₁ + 6x₁(1 − x₁), so dV/dx₁ = 22 + 6 − 12x₁ = 28 − 12x₁.
examples.answer: V̄₁ = 43.375 cm³/mol and V̄₂ = 18.375 cm³/mol at x₁ = 0.25.
examples.check:
x1=0.25
x2=1-x1
V=40*x1+18*x2+6*x1*x2
dVdx1=40-18+6*(1-2*x1)
V1=V+x2*dVdx1
V2=V-x1*dVdx1
print(V)
print(dVdx1)
print(V1)
print(V2)

traps: Using pure-component V₁ and V₂ in V = x₁V₁ + x₂V₂. The sum needs V̄₁ and V̄₂ at the mixture composition; pure values are valid only at x<sub>i</sub> = 1.
Dropping the fixed variables in M̄<sub>i</sub> = (∂(nM)/∂n<sub>i</sub>). The derivative is at constant T, P and all other n<sub>j</sub>, not at constant total n alone.
Mixing the signs in the binary formulas. M̄₁ has +x₂ dM/dx₁; M̄₂ has −x₁ dM/dx₁. Reversing them swaps the two intercepts.
Differentiating M instead of nM. The definition uses the extensive property nM; for molar M the same result follows only after the n<sub>i</sub> dependence of x<sub>i</sub> is handled.
Treating μ<sub>i</sub> as the pure Gibbs energy. μ<sub>i</sub> equals Ḡ<sub>i</sub>, the partial molar Gibbs energy at the mixture composition.

quiz.q: Define a partial molar property M̄<sub>i</sub> by its derivative.
quiz.a: M̄<sub>i</sub> = (∂(nM)/∂n<sub>i</sub>)<sub>T,P,n<sub>j</sub></sub>, where nM is the total extensive property and other moles are fixed.

quiz.q: Why can the partial molar volume of water in ethanol differ from the molar volume of pure water?
quiz.a: The surrounding ethanol molecules change water's interactions and packing. Adding water changes the mixture volume non-additively; the pure value applies only at x<sub>water</sub> = 1.

quiz.q: For V = 30x₁ + 20x₂ + 4x₁x₂ at x₁ = 0.2, find V̄₁ and V̄₂.
At x₁ = 0.3, M = 25 and dM/dx₁ = −8. Find M̄₁ and M̄₂.
quiz.a: M̄₁ = 25 + 0.7(−8) = 19.4. M̄₂ = 25 − 0.3(−8) = 27.4. The negative slope makes component 2's partial value larger.

quiz.q: State the relation between mixture M and partial molar values.
quiz.a: M = Σ x<sub>i</sub> M̄<sub>i</sub> at fixed T and P, summed over all components.

quiz.q: For V = 18 + 28x − 6x² at x = 0.5, find V̄₁ and V̄₂.
Why does the tangent intercept on an M versus x₁ plot equal a partial molar property?
quiz.a: Let X be the mole fraction read along the axis. The tangent at x₁ is y(X) = M + (dM/dx₁)(X − x₁), and dM/dx₁ = M̄₁ − M̄₂. At X = 1, y = M + x₂(dM/dx₁) = M̄₁; at X = 0, y = M − x₁(dM/dx₁) = M̄₂.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store partial molar properties internally when they convert density and calorimetry data into component Gibbs energies. Polymer and electrolyte solutions need composition-dependent partial molar volumes because their molecules change size and charge interactions. Modern software uses group-contribution and quantum-chemistry methods to estimate these values when data are scarce. Search for partial molar volume, tangent-intercept method, and excess partial molar properties.
